title: Finding a Gene by What It Does
endLine: Split pools of expressed genes until one alone creates the response.

scenes.tts: A sensory neuron responds to capsaicin, the burning chemical in chilli peppers. Which gene makes it react? That cell expresses many genes at once, none carrying labels. You cannot spot the sensor by looking at D N A alone. Instead, you find the gene by what it does.
scenes.caption: A sensory neuron responds to capsaicin, the burning chemical in chilli peppers. Which gene makes it react? That cell expresses many genes at once, none carrying labels. You cannot spot the sensor by looking at DNA alone. Instead, you find the gene by what it does.
scenes.visual: Schematic. A large sensory nerve ending fills most of the frame height; capsaicin drops land on its membrane and the ending glows bright gold. Zoom inside to a drifting crowd of unlabeled gene ribbons, with one pulsing faintly beside a large question mark.
scenes.narration: A sensory neuron responds to capsaicin, the burning chemical in chilli peppers. Which gene makes it react? That cell expresses many genes at once, none carrying labels. You cannot spot the sensor by looking at DNA alone. Instead, you find the gene by what it does.

scenes.visual: Title card 'Finding a Gene by What It Does' fades in cleanly over the slowly drifting unlabeled gene crowd, then fades out as the crowd gathers into a ribbon across the top of the frame.

scenes.tts: First, make D N A copies of the tissue's expressed genes, called c D N A. Divide them into pools. Next, pick foreign cells, like H E K two ninety three, that do not normally respond to capsaicin. Putting a gene into foreign cells is heterologous expression.
scenes.caption: First, make DNA copies of the tissue's expressed genes, called cDNA. Divide them into pools. Next, pick foreign cells, like HEK293, that do not normally respond to capsaicin. Putting a gene into foreign cells is heterologous expression.
scenes.visual: Schematic, same stage. The gene ribbon at top copies into cDNA strands and sorts into labeled pools above a tray of large dark HEK293 cells filling most of the frame height. A test drop of capsaicin lands on the bare cells; they stay dark.
scenes.narration: First, make DNA copies of the tissue's expressed genes, called cDNA. Divide them into pools. Next, pick foreign cells, like HEK293, that do not normally respond to capsaicin. Putting a gene into foreign cells is heterologous expression.

scenes.tts: Now put one pool into each dish of silent foreign cells. Give the cells time to make the encoded proteins. Then add capsaicin and watch for calcium flowing into the cells. Most dishes stay dark, lacking the sensor. One dish glows, marking the winning pool.
scenes.caption: Now put one pool into each dish of silent foreign cells. Give the cells time to make the encoded proteins. Then add capsaicin and watch for calcium flowing into the cells. Most dishes stay dark, lacking the sensor. One dish glows, marking the winning pool.
scenes.visual: Schematic, same tray. Each pool pours down into its own well of dark cells; small dots appear on cell membranes as proteins are made. The dropper releases capsaicin across every well. All wells stay dark except one, which fills with a bright gold calcium glow.
scenes.narration: Now put one pool into each dish of silent foreign cells. Give the cells time to make the encoded proteins. Then add capsaicin and watch for calcium flowing into the cells. Most dishes stay dark, lacking the sensor. One dish glows, marking the winning pool.

scenes.tts: That glowing dish still holds a whole pool of genes. Split the winning pool into smaller pools and test fresh silent cells. Repeat this narrowing until one clone remains. That is expression cloning: split pools of expressed genes until one alone creates the response.
scenes.caption: That glowing dish still holds a whole pool of genes. Split the winning pool into smaller pools and test fresh silent cells. Repeat this narrowing until one clone remains. That is expression cloning: split pools of expressed genes until one alone creates the response.
scenes.visual: Schematic, same tray. The winning pool lifts from the glowing well, splits into smaller sub-pools, and pours into fresh dark wells. Capsaicin drops again; one smaller well glows. A final split leaves one highlighted gene making a single cell glow bright gold.
scenes.narration: That glowing dish still holds a whole pool of genes. Split the winning pool into smaller pools and test fresh silent cells. Repeat this narrowing until one clone remains. That is expression cloning: split pools of expressed genes until one alone creates the response.

scenes.tts: Suppose your single cloned gene makes a foreign cell respond to capsaicin and noxious heat. Pause and think before we go on. Does that prove an intact animal actually needs this gene to sense heat?
scenes.caption: Suppose your single cloned gene makes a foreign cell respond to capsaicin and noxious heat. Pause and think before we go on. Does that prove an intact animal actually needs this gene to sense heat?
scenes.visual: Schematic. The single glowing foreign cell slides left; a silhouette of an intact mouse fades in on the right with a large question mark between them. High-contrast question text appears above: 'Does an intact animal need this gene?'
scenes.narration: Suppose your single cloned gene makes a foreign cell respond to capsaicin and noxious heat. Pause and think before we go on. Does that prove an intact animal actually needs this gene to sense heat?

scenes.visual: Schematic. The question stays crisp on screen for a thinking pause while the glowing foreign cell on the left shimmers gently and the question mark over the intact mouse pulses slowly.

scenes.tts: No. Cloning shows a gene is sufficient: it gives a foreign cell the response. It does not prove the animal needs it, or that it works alone. Testing need means removing the gene. In 2018, Vandewauw and colleagues showed three heat channels act in parallel. Single removals kept acute heat withdrawal; only losing all three abolished it.
scenes.caption: No. Cloning shows a gene is sufficient: it gives a foreign cell the response. It does not prove the animal needs it, or that it works alone. Testing need means removing the gene. In 2018, Vandewauw and colleagues showed three heat channels act in parallel. Single removals kept acute heat withdrawal; only losing all three abolished it.
scenes.visual: Schematic, same split stage. The glowing foreign cell on the left gets the label 'Sufficient'. The intact mouse on the right splits into three parallel paths labeled TRPV1, TRPM3, and TRPA1 (Vandewauw 2018): cutting one path leaves the withdrawal arrow lit; cutting all three turns it dark.
scenes.narration: No. Cloning shows a gene is sufficient: it gives a foreign cell the response. It does not prove the animal needs it, or that it works alone. Testing need means removing the gene. In 2018, Vandewauw and colleagues showed three heat channels act in parallel. Single removals kept acute heat withdrawal; only losing all three abolished it.

scenes.tts: Controls for expression itself check that the procedure alone did not cause the effect. Removing a gene from the start also lets development compensate. And making a cell pass current never proves the protein lines the pore. Necessity, sufficiency and pore identity are three separate claims.
scenes.caption: Controls for expression itself check that the procedure alone did not cause the effect. Removing a gene from the start also lets development compensate. And making a cell pass current never proves the protein lines the pore. Necessity, sufficiency and pore identity are three separate claims.
scenes.visual: Schematic, same tray. Three concise checks appear in turn over the carried stage: a control well stays dark beside the active well; the mouse outline gains a 'Development compensates' tag; a membrane pore zooms to three stacked tags: 'Sufficient', 'Necessary', 'Lines pore'.
scenes.narration: Controls for expression itself check that the procedure alone did not cause the effect. Removing a gene from the start also lets development compensate. And making a cell pass current never proves the protein lines the pore. Necessity, sufficiency and pore identity are three separate claims.

scenes.tts: With those checks, expression cloning unlocked landmark proteins. In 1992, Smith and Harland injected R N A pools into ultraviolet-treated embryos lacking dorsal structures. Narrowing the pools found Noggin, which rescued them. In 1997, He and Tessier-Lavigne screened c D N A pools for cells binding a tagged cue. They found neuropilin, the receiver of Sema three A, a repulsive cue.
scenes.caption: With those checks, expression cloning unlocked landmark proteins. In 1992, Smith and Harland injected RNA pools into ultraviolet-treated embryos lacking dorsal structures. Narrowing the pools found Noggin, which rescued them. In 1997, He and Tessier-Lavigne screened cDNA pools for cells binding a tagged cue. They found neuropilin, the receiver of Sema3A, a repulsive cue.
scenes.visual: Schematic, same pool-narrowing stage. First, RNA pools narrow into a spherical embryo that regrows a dorsal ridge, tagged 'Noggin, 1992'. Next, the stage shifts back to cells in wells; a tagged cue sticks to one glowing well, tagged 'Neuropilin, 1997'.
scenes.narration: With those checks, expression cloning unlocked landmark proteins. In 1992, Smith and Harland injected RNA pools into ultraviolet-treated embryos lacking dorsal structures. Narrowing the pools found Noggin, which rescued them. In 1997, He and Tessier-Lavigne screened cDNA pools for cells binding a tagged cue. They found neuropilin, the receiver of Sema3A, a repulsive cue.

scenes.tts: Also in 1997, Caterina and colleagues in David Julius's laboratory answered our opening question. They screened sensory-neuron c D N A pools for capsaicin-evoked calcium influx. The clone they recovered, T R P V one, encoded a channel also activated by noxious heating. Whenever a response hides its gene, narrow expressed pools until one reproduces it.
scenes.caption: Also in 1997, Caterina and colleagues in David Julius's laboratory answered our opening question. They screened sensory-neuron cDNA pools for capsaicin-evoked calcium influx. The clone they recovered, TRPV1, encoded a channel also activated by noxious heating. Whenever a response hides its gene, narrow expressed pools until one reproduces it.
scenes.visual: Schematic, same tray. Sensory-neuron cDNA pools narrow to one glowing cell under capsaicin drops and heat waves, tagged 'TRPV1, 1997'. The pool funnel and single glowing cell stay centered, settling calmly as the screen clears for the end card.
scenes.narration: Also in 1997, Caterina and colleagues in David Julius's laboratory answered our opening question. They screened sensory-neuron cDNA pools for capsaicin-evoked calcium influx. The clone they recovered, TRPV1, encoded a channel also activated by noxious heating. Whenever a response hides its gene, narrow expressed pools until one reproduces it.

scenes.visual: Clean end card displaying the take-home rule in large high-contrast text: 'Split pools of expressed genes until one alone creates the response.'
